chunks: And Harun ibn Hamzah narrated from Ali ibn Abdul Aziz who said:
Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: "What has Umar ibn Muslim done?" I said: "May I be your ransom, he has devoted himself to worship and abandoned trade."

He said: "Woe to him! Does he not know that the one who abandons seeking sustenance will not have his supplication answered? Indeed, a group of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), when the verse was revealed: 'And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out and provide for him from where he does not expect,' locked their doors and devoted themselves to worship, saying, 'We have been guaranteed provision.' When this reached the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), he sent for them and said: 'What led you to do what you have done?' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, Allah, the Mighty and Exalted, has guaranteed our provision, so we have devoted ourselves to worship.' He said: 'Indeed, whoever does this, Allah will not answer his supplication. You must continue seeking sustenance.'
Then he said: "I hate a man who is impious, opening his mouth to his Lord, saying, 'Provide for me,' while he abandons seeking sustenance."

key_terms.أَصْحَابِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ: Companions of the Messenger of Allah

ai.seo_question: Why does abandoning work and trade prevent a person's supplications from being answered?
ai.summary: This hadith from Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih highlights the Shia jurisprudential balance between spiritual devotion and economic activity, warning against 'passive reliance' (tawakkul bi-l-qalb) without physical effort. It contextualizes the Companions' reaction to Surah At-Talaq 65:2, illustrating that divine promise of provision does not negate the obligation of active pursuit (talab), a principle central to Islamic commercial ethics.
